content.text: Preserve's 500s line up with the POST that returns 401. Before going further I need the metric schemas, so I can check resource signals on the other changed services.

input.query: SELECT c.service_name caller, c.attr_k8s_pod_name cpod, c.span_name cname, s.service_name callee, count(*) n, round(avg(c.duration)/1e6,1) c_ms, sum(CASE WHEN s.attr_span_kind IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) no_child FROM abnormal_traces c LEFT JOIN abnormal_traces s ON c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND s.parent_span_id=c.span_id AND s.attr_span_kind='Server' WHERE c.service_name='ts-preserve-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC

content.text: The failing call is preserve's POST to seat-service: the client span shows 401 while seat's own server span returns 200, so the status is altered on the caller side. Next I'll break down the user-facing endpoints on ui-dashboard and the slow downstream services.

input.query: SELECT CASE WHEN trace_id IS NULL THEN 'x' ELSE 'ab' END p, service_name, span_name, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,1) p50, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-ui-dashboard' AND attr_span_kind='Server' GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'norm', service_name, span_name, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,1), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-ui-dashboard' AND attr_span_kind='Server' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 3,1

content.text: The user-facing ui-dashboard endpoints (routes, trains, users, contacts, consigns, foods) all got slower. Next I'll compare resource metrics per service between normal and abnormal periods.

input.query: WITH n AS (SELECT service_name s, metric m, avg(value) v FROM normal_metrics GROUP BY 1,2 UNION ALL SELECT service_name, metric, avg(value) FROM normal_metrics_sum GROUP BY 1,2), a AS (SELECT service_name s, metric m, avg(value) v FROM abnormal_metrics GROUP BY 1,2 UNION ALL SELECT service_name, metric, avg(value) FROM abnormal_metrics_sum GROUP BY 1,2) SELECT a.s, a.m, round(n.v,2) nv, round(a.v,2) av, round(a.v/nullif(n.v,0),2) ratio FROM a JOIN n USING (s,m) WHERE abs(a.v - n.v) > 0.3*abs(n.v) + 0.01 AND a.s LIKE 'ts-%' ORDER BY abs(ln(abs(a.v/nullif(n.v,0)+1e-9))) DESC

content.text: In that route-plan trace, about 4.4 s of the 6.6 s server time is not in any child call, so route-plan's own code is slow. I'll look at its internal spans.

input.query: SELECT 'ab' p, span_name, attr_span_kind, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,1) p50, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-route-plan-service' GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'nm', span_name, attr_span_kind, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,1), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-route-plan-service' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,1

content.text: Route-plan's own controller time was already high in the normal period and only shifts moderately, so it is probably downstream of something else. I'll check the callees of the slow travel services (travel2, travel, basic) to find where the time goes.

input.query: SELECT p.service_name caller, p.span_name pname, c.service_name callee, c.span_name cname, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.5)/1e6,1) c_p50, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.95)/1e6,1) c_p95, round(quantile_cont(p.duration,0.5)/1e6,1) p_p50 FROM abnormal_traces p JOIN abnormal_traces c ON c.trace_id=p.trace_id AND c.parent_span_id=p.span_id WHERE p.service_name IN ('ts-travel2-service','ts-travel-service','ts-basic-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-food-service','ts-auth-service','ts-ui-dashboard') AND p.attr_span_kind='Client' AND c.attr_span_kind='Server' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1,3,2

content.text: Latency is up broadly across callees (seat, basic, route, travel), which suggests a shared resource rather than one service. I'll list the metric names and check per-pod CPU and throttling.

input.query: SELECT metric, count(*) n, count(DISTINCT service_name) svcs FROM (SELECT * FROM abnormal_metrics UNION ALL SELECT * FROM abnormal_metrics_sum) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

content.text: Next I'll compare pod CPU-limit utilisation and restart counts per service between periods.

input.query: SELECT metric, service_name, round(avg(CASE WHEN src='n' THEN value END),3) nv, round(avg(CASE WHEN src='a' THEN value END),3) av, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN src='a' THEN attr_k8s_pod_name END) apods FROM (SELECT 'n' src, * FROM normal_metrics UNION ALL SELECT 'a', * FROM abnormal_metrics) WHERE metric IN ('k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization','k8s.pod.memory_limit_utilization','k8s.pod.uptime','k8s.pod.cpu.node.utilization','container.memory.page_faults','queueSize') AND service_name IN ('ts-preserve-service','ts-basic-service','ts-seat-service','ts-route-service','ts-travel-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-station-food-service','ts-food-service','ts-security-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-auth-service','ts-order-service','ts-ui-dashboard','ts-contacts-service','ts-price-service','ts-train-service') GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

content.text: Pod-level CPU and memory are mostly flat, so the slowdowns are request-path effects. The hubble HTTP duration metrics moved a lot for some connections, so I'll break those down by source and destination.

input.query: SELECT metric, attr_source, attr_destination, round(avg(CASE WHEN src='n' THEN value END),3) nv, round(avg(CASE WHEN src='a' THEN value END),3) av FROM (SELECT 'n' src, * FROM normal_metrics UNION ALL SELECT 'a', * FROM abnormal_metrics) WHERE metric='hubble_http_request_duration_p95_seconds' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY av DESC NULLS LAST

SELECT metric, attr_source_workload src_w, attr_destination_workload dst_w, attr_source sp, attr_destination dp, round(avg(CASE WHEN tag='n' THEN value END),3) nv, round(avg(CASE WHEN tag='a' THEN value END),3) av, count(*) rows_ FROM (SELECT 'n' tag, * FROM normal_metrics_sum UNION ALL SELECT 'a', * FROM abnormal_metrics_sum) WHERE metric LIKE 'hubble_%' AND metric IN ('hubble_drop_total','hubble_http_requests_total') GROUP BY ALL HAVING av IS NOT NULL OR nv IS NOT NULL ORDER BY abs(coalesce(av,0)-coalesce(nv,0)) DESC

content.text: Hubble request counts simply track the traffic shift, so they don't point to a network fault. Next I'll inspect station-food's self time in individual traces to decide between a DB-call fault and an application-method fault.

input.query: WITH t AS (SELECT trace_id FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-station-food-service' AND attr_span_kind='Server' ORDER BY duration DESC LIMIT 2) SELECT service_name, span_name, attr_span_kind kind, parent_span_id = '' root, span_id, parent_span_id, round(duration/1e6,1) ms, time FROM abnormal_traces WHERE trace_id IN (SELECT trace_id FROM t) AND service_name IN ('ts-station-food-service','ts-food-service') ORDER BY trace_id, time

Other investigators, each starting fresh with the same tools, checked your draft answer: the kind of each fault, and how each fault's effect travelled. Their findings:

### `ts-preserve-service`: you said `http_wrong_status_code`. They agree (confidence: medium).
Scope: Affected: only ts-preserve-service's outgoing POST to ts-seat-service /api/v1/seatservice/seats, where the client span records 401 on all 537 calls while seat's Server span for the same call returns 200. Preserve's 500 responses and its SEVERE logs on the same 537 requests are downstream of that status. Not affected: preserve's other outgoing calls (POST to travel, POST to basic, GET to contacts, GET to security), seat's own processing and status codes, and the preserve-seat network connection, which shows no drops.
Ruled out:
- `network_delay`: The client span for the seat POST averages 35.6 ms against 24.2 ms for the seat Server span, so there is no large unexplained gap on the wire, and the calls complete with a valid status rather than being slowed. Hubble flows between preserve and seat rose about 5x with zero drops, so the connection is live and not delayed.
- `network_loss`: The hubble drop counters for the preserve-seat pair stay at 0.0, and every seat call returns a complete HTTP response with a status. There are no retransmit or timeout signatures on the seat calls.
- `network_partition`: Calls are not hanging or failing to connect. Every seat call gets a 401 response and a matching seat Server span, so the connection is not cut.
- `network_corrupt`: The calls complete with a parseable HTTP status, and there are no deserialization or checksum errors in the traces. Nothing indicates altered bytes at the transport level.
- `http_aborted`: An aborted exchange would not produce a clean, complete 401 that matches a 200 at the far end. Every seat POST ends with a status code and a Server span, so the HTTP exchange is not cut.
- `http_response_body_corrupted`: The only divergence in the traces is the status code. No body or path change is visible, though no response bodies are captured, so this is not fully excluded and is the main residual alternative.
- `wrong_return_value`: The 401 is recorded by the HTTP client instrumentation on the preserve side, so it came from the wire, not from preserve's own return value. Seat's Server span shows 200, so the value was not produced inside seat either.
- `application_exception`: Preserve's Internal spans other than PreserveController.preserve are not in error, and the error is tied to the status code of the outgoing call, not to an exception thrown in application code.
- `database_call_failed`: Preserve's errors are HTTP status codes on the seat call and the 500 response, with no SQL-layer error text associated with them.
- `database_call_slow`: The seat Server span's own time fell from 24.0 ms to 11.6 ms, and the calls are not slow, so there is no database-bound latency.
- `application_method_slow`: Preserve's self time fell from 37 ms to 14 ms, and seat's own processing is unchanged, so no method is growing in self time.
- `http_slow`: Seat's Server span returns in 24 ms and the client span in 35 ms, so there is no application-layer hold-back at HTTP level.
- `pod_failure`: Seat keeps answering with 200 on its Server spans, and no restart or gap in seat's signals is shown, so seat is not down.
- `pod_unavailable`: Seat continues to emit Server spans with 200 status for the same calls, so the instance is not gone.
- `dns_lookup_failed`: The calls reach seat and return a response, and there is no name-resolution error text.
- `dns_returned_wrong_address`: Seat's Server span exists for each of the 537 preserve calls, so requests reach the intended peer.
- `container_cpu_saturated`: The CPU shifts in the survey are not tied to the seat error, and seat's latency is normal, so there is no resource-bound slowdown.
- `container_memory_saturated`: No memory-pressure signal is linked to the 401 responses, and seat's latency is normal.
- `jvm_heap_exhausted`: No heap-exhaustion signal is linked to the 401 responses, and seat's own processing is normal.
- `jvm_gc_thrashing`: Seat's own processing time is normal, so there is no GC stall tied to the status errors.
- `process_cpu_saturated`: Seat's own processing time is normal, so there is no process-level CPU stall tied to the status errors.
Evidence:
- All 537 preserve-to-seat POST client spans record 401, and each joins to a seat Server span for POST /api/v1/seatservice/seats with status 200. The other preserve outgoing calls (to travel, basic, contacts, security) all return 200. The client span averages 35.6 ms and the seat Server span 24.2 ms.
  `SELECT c.service_name caller, c.span_name, c.attr_http_response_status_code client_code, s.service_name callee, s.span_name server_span, s.attr_http_response_status_code server_code, s.attr_span_kind sk, count(*) n, avg(c.duration)/1e6 c_ms, avg(s.duration)/1e6 s_ms FROM abnormal_traces c LEFT JOIN abnormal_traces s ON c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND s.parent_span_id=c.span_id WHERE c.service_name='ts-preserve-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC`
- In the abnormal period preserve's Server span for POST /api/v1/preserveservice/preserve returns 500 with Error status on 537 requests. PreserveController.preserve (Internal) is in Error on 537 requests, BasicErrorController.error runs on 537, and the outgoing POST client span with 401 is Error on 537. The downstream 401 matches the upstream 500 one-to-one.
  `SELECT 'abn' p, service_name, span_name, attr_span_kind, attr_http_response_status_code code, attr_status_code, count(*) n FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-preserve-service' GROUP BY ALL`
- Exactly 537 preserve POST client spans carry status 401, which is the same count as the 500 responses and the seat-call mismatches, so the status error is confined to this single outgoing route.
  `SELECT 'trace_preserve_401_mismatch' t, span_name, CAST(attr_http_response_status_code AS VARCHAR) code, count(*) n FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-preserve-service' AND attr_span_kind='Client' AND span_name='POST' AND attr_http_response_status_code=401 GROUP BY ALL`
- Preserve logs 537 SEVERE entries in the abnormal period, against none in normal. Seat logs only INFO. The SEVERE entries are on the failing preserve path, so the error is contained to preserve's handling of the seat response.
  `SELECT service_name, level, count(*) n, any_value(CAST(trace_id AS VARCHAR)) ex FROM abnormal_logs WHERE service_name IN ('ts-preserve-service','ts-seat-service') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC`

### `ts-station-food-service`: you said `database_call_slow`. They conclude `network_loss` (confidence: low).
Scope: Affected: the ts-station-food-service DB call to its station_food_store table (store p95 1.9 to 50.6 ms, with a bursty tail and flat median) and, to a smaller degree, the list statement on the same DB connection (p95 1.8 to 11.1 ms, median flat). Also affected is the food-to-station-food call as seen from the server side, with server p95 rising from 24 to 185 ms, mostly inside station-food's handler. Not shown affected: station-food's CPU and memory (CPU down, memory flat), its continued emission of spans through the abnormal window (no gap), and the station-food to mysql hubble TCP flags (unchanged at 20). The lead's claim that the list query is unchanged does not hold in the data.
Ruled out:
- `database_call_slow`: Claimed kind rejected. The store statement's median is flat (0.66 to 0.73 ms) while its p95 jumps, and the tail is bursty (one minute p95 86 ms with p50 0.93 ms, others near 0.5 ms), not a steady per-statement shift. The list statement on the same DB connection also gets a p95 tail (1.8 to 11.1 ms, max 27 ms), so the fault is not confined to one statement kind. Sibling service ts-station-service also shows DB-statement tail growth (SELECT station p95 3.0 to 15.5 ms).
- `application_method_slow`: The growth in StationFoodController and StationFoodRepository spans is almost entirely the DB-call span's time; the non-DB own time is small. Station-food's own p95 rose 3.3 to 18.4 ms, far less than the DB-call tail, and the rise is not attributed to a self-timed method.
- `network_delay`: Extra time on the wire would add a similar amount to every call on the connection. The food-to-station-food client-minus-server gap at p50 grew only from about 4.4 to 7.7 ms, and the store tail is irregular with a flat median, not a uniform added latency. Hubble flows to mysql rose only modestly and no drops appear.
- `http_slow`: The slowdown is in the DB-call spans on station-food's own connection, not held back at the HTTP layer of a particular route; the route's Server span time is explained by its child DB spans.
- `container_cpu_saturated`: Station-food pod CPU usage fell from 0.04 to 0.01 cores in the abnormal period, so the container is not CPU-pinned.
- `process_cpu_saturated`: Same metric as container CPU: the pod's CPU usage fell, leaving no sign of a single-process CPU saturation.
- `container_memory_saturated`: Pod working-set memory was flat (about 764 MB normal vs 770 MB abnormal, max 771 MB against a normal max of 769 MB).
- `pod_unavailable`: Station-food kept emitting spans in the abnormal period (about 40 per minute), and the store and list statements run in every minute of the window, so the instance was not gone.
- `pod_failure`: No gap-then-recovery pattern in station-food's span emission. Restart and uptime metrics were not returned for this service, so a restart cannot be confirmed either way, but the continuous span stream argues against a pod-lifecycle fault.
Evidence:
- Store and list Client spans on the station-food to mysql path have flat medians (about 0.3 to 1.5 ms) in every minute, but p95 tails jump irregularly: store at 04:42 p95 85.9 ms with p50 0.93 ms, at 04:43 p95 0.7 ms; list at 04:42 p95 26.9 ms with p50 0.68 ms. The pattern is bursty, not a steady per-statement slowdown.
  `SELECT span_name, attr_span_kind, date_trunc('minute', time) m, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,2) p50, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,2) p95, round(min(duration)/1e6,2) mn FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-station-food-service' AND span_name IN ('SELECT ts.station_food_store','SELECT ts.station_food_list') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY m, span_name`
- Store Client span p50 0.66 to 0.73 ms, p95 1.93 to 50.59 ms (n 94 to 17). List Client span p50 0.40 to 0.46 ms, p95 1.81 to 11.13 ms (n 402 to 75). Station-food Server span p95 23.81 to 185.03 ms, with its StationFoodController span p95 19.6 to 181.8 ms.

- Food-to-station-food call pairs: normal client p50 14.33 ms vs server p50 9.97 ms (gap about 4.4 ms); abnormal client p50 22.53 ms vs server p50 14.81 ms (gap about 7.7 ms). Server p95 rose 23.8 to 185.0 ms; client p95 rose 55.1 to 193.4 ms. The added time sits mostly inside the server handler, with only a small growth in the wire gap.
  `SELECT c.attr_span_kind ck, c.span_name, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.5)/1e6,2) client_p50, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.95)/1e6,2) client_p95, round(quantile_cont(s.duration,0.5)/1e6,2) server_p50, round(quantile_cont(s.duration,0.95)/1e6,2) server_p95, count(*) n FROM abnormal_traces c JOIN abnormal_traces s ON s.parent_span_id = c.span_id AND s.attr_span_kind='Server' WHERE c.service_name='ts-food-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND s.service_name='ts-station-food-service' GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT c.attr_span_kind, c.span_name, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.5)/1e6,2), round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.95)/1e6,2), round(quantile_cont(s.duration,0.5)/1e6,2), round(quantile_cont(s.duration,0.95)/1e6,2), count(*) FROM normal_traces c JOIN normal_traces s ON s.parent_span_id = c.span_id AND s.attr_span_kind='Server' WHERE c.service_name='ts-food-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND s.service_name='ts-station-food-service' GROUP BY ALL`

**Verdict: the evidence supports `http_wrong_status_code`, with the fault on preserve's POST to seat-service. Confidence is medium-high.** The telemetry cannot show whether the rewrite happened on the wire or in a filter between seat's instrumentation and preserve's client, and no response bodies are recorded, so body changes cannot be excluded.

**What I checked**

- **Status mismatch on one call.** All 537 preserve→seat POST client spans record 401 with `attr_status_code=Error`. Each one joins to a seat Server span (`POST /api/v1/seatservice/seats`) that records 200. Seat's Server spans in the abnormal period are all 200 and none are errors. Seat itself is not reporting failure, so the 401 did not originate in seat's response.
- **Scope is one route on one peer.** Preserve's other outgoing calls in the same window are clean: POST to travel `trip_detail`, POST to basic, GET to contacts and GET to security all return 200 with no error status. The fault is not on the whole connection or the whole pod.
- **Body intact is not contradicted, but not shown.** Nothing in the traces indicates a changed body. Seat's normal 200 and the clean downstream path support a status-only change, though no body was captured.
- **Consequence matches the kind.** Preserve's `PreserveController.preserve` Internal span is in error on 537 requests. Its Server span returns 500 on the same 537, with a `BasicErrorController.error` child. Preserve logs 537 SEVERE entries. The 500 is the downstream effect of treating the 401 as a failure. The lead's one-to-one count is correct.

**Alternatives checked against the data**

- **`network_loss`, `network_partition`, `network_delay` or `network_corrupt`.** Hubble shows preserve↔seat flows rising about 5×, with zero drops on every pair. The client span takes 35 ms against 24 ms for the seat Server span, so there is no large unexplained wire gap. The calls are not hanging or timing out, and the call completes with a valid status. These are ruled out.
- **`http_aborted`.** An aborted exchange would not produce a clean, complete 401 with a matching 200 at the far end. Ruled out.
- **`http_response_body_corrupted`.** The status is the only thing the telemetry shows as changed. I found no body or path evidence either way. This is the main residual alternative, and it can only be settled with body capture.
- **`wrong_return_value` in preserve.** The 401 is recorded by the HTTP client instrumentation, so it came from the wire, not from preserve's own return value. Seat's own 200 points away from a seat-side fault. Unlikely.
- **`application_exception`, `database_call_failed`, `*_method_slow`.** Preserve's internal spans other than the controller are normal. Seat's own time is unchanged. Not supported.
- **Pod faults or resource saturation.** No restarts are reported, and the survey's largest metric shifts on preserve (filesystem usage, 63.8 normal-SDs) do not line up with a resource fault that would slow every outgoing call. Seat's JVM metric shift is also not tied to this error. Not supported.

**Notes on the survey**

- The "error share 0.38" on preserve and the "1.00" error share on ui-dashboard→preserve are downstream propagation of the 401, not separate faults.
- Preserve's own p95 falls from 37 ms to 14 ms in self-time, consistent with fast failure rather than slowness.

**What would firm this up:** response body or header capture for the seat POST, or a proxy/filter trace between seat and preserve. Either would separate a status-only rewrite from a body rewrite.

kind_checks.scope: Affected: the ts-station-food-service DB call to its station_food_store table (store p95 1.9 to 50.6 ms, with a bursty tail and flat median) and, to a smaller degree, the list statement on the same DB connection (p95 1.8 to 11.1 ms, median flat). Also affected is the food-to-station-food call as seen from the server side, with server p95 rising from 24 to 185 ms, mostly inside station-food's handler. Not shown affected: station-food's CPU and memory (CPU down, memory flat), its continued emission of spans through the abnormal window (no gap), and the station-food to mysql hubble TCP flags (unchanged at 20). The lead's claim that the list query is unchanged does not hold in the data.

ruled_out.why: Claimed kind rejected. The store statement's median is flat (0.66 to 0.73 ms) while its p95 jumps, and the tail is bursty (one minute p95 86 ms with p50 0.93 ms, others near 0.5 ms), not a steady per-statement shift. The list statement on the same DB connection also gets a p95 tail (1.8 to 11.1 ms, max 27 ms), so the fault is not confined to one statement kind. Sibling service ts-station-service also shows DB-statement tail growth (SELECT station p95 3.0 to 15.5 ms).

The growth in StationFoodController and StationFoodRepository spans is almost entirely the DB-call span's time; the non-DB own time is small. Station-food's own p95 rose 3.3 to 18.4 ms, far less than the DB-call tail, and the rise is not attributed to a self-timed method.

Extra time on the wire would add a similar amount to every call on the connection. The food-to-station-food client-minus-server gap at p50 grew only from about 4.4 to 7.7 ms, and the store tail is irregular with a flat median, not a uniform added latency. Hubble flows to mysql rose only modestly and no drops appear.
The slowdown is in the DB-call spans on station-food's own connection, not held back at the HTTP layer of a particular route; the route's Server span time is explained by its child DB spans.
Station-food pod CPU usage fell from 0.04 to 0.01 cores in the abnormal period, so the container is not CPU-pinned.
Same metric as container CPU: the pod's CPU usage fell, leaving no sign of a single-process CPU saturation.
Pod working-set memory was flat (about 764 MB normal vs 770 MB abnormal, max 771 MB against a normal max of 769 MB).
Station-food kept emitting spans in the abnormal period (about 40 per minute), and the store and list statements run in every minute of the window, so the instance was not gone.

No gap-then-recovery pattern in station-food's span emission. Restart and uptime metrics were not returned for this service, so a restart cannot be confirmed either way, but the continuous span stream argues against a pod-lifecycle fault.

content.text:
**Verdict: `database_call_slow` is not supported as stated.** The evidence does not fit a steady slowdown confined to station-food's store statements. The affected tail is on the connection and in other statements too, which points to a connection-level fault. I'd put low-to-moderate confidence on a network-class fault (loss/partition is the equivalence class that fits the irregular tail best). The telemetry does not cleanly separate it from a database-side problem.

**What I checked (about 9 queries)**

1. **Store statement shape.** `SELECT ts.station_food_store` Client: p50 0.66 → 0.73 ms (flat), p95 1.9 → 50.6 ms. The minute-by-minute view is bursty: one minute at p95 86 ms with p50 0.93, another at p50 12 ms, while other minutes are back at ~0.5 ms. A steady per-statement slowdown would move the median. This shape matches irregular times with long tails.

2. **The list query is not unchanged.** The lead says it is, but `SELECT ts.station_food_list` Client p95 went 1.81 → 11.13 ms, with a minute at p95 26.9 ms and max 27 ms. The median is flat (0.40 → 0.46 ms). So the other statement on the same DB connection also shows a tail. `database_call_slow` requires other statements on the connection to stay normal.

3. **Other DB clients are also hit.** `ts-station-service` (a different service with its own DB use) shows its own statement tails: `SELECT station` p95 2.99 → 15.5 ms, `StationRepository.findByNames` p95 4.0 → 16.2 ms, with medians roughly flat. That suggests shared database or path-level behaviour, not something inside station-food's own driver. It is a caveat, not proof, since station-service's spans could also reflect its own load.

4. **Where the time sits in the call.** Food → station-food: Server span p95 23.8 → 185 ms, and the Client-minus-Server gap at the median grew from about 4.4 ms to 7.7 ms. The growth is mostly inside station-food's handler: the Server, `StationFoodController` and `StationFoodRepository` spans all carry it. That is consistent with a DB wait, and it is also consistent with the call being slow on the wire. The span data alone does not separate the two.

5. **Network counters.** The station-food ↔ mysql hubble flows rose only modestly (42 → 54 avg), TCP flag counts to mysql are unchanged (20 both), and no drops appear on any station-food link in either period. Pod network error metrics are absent for this service, so retransmission or loss cannot be confirmed or ruled out from metrics.

6. **Pod-level metrics.** Station-food CPU usage fell (0.04 → 0.01 cores); memory working set is flat (~765 MB → ~770 MB). No CPU or memory saturation. Restart, uptime and ready metrics were not returned for this service, so I cannot confirm a pod-lifecycle event; I am treating them as missing.

**Survey points I'd flag.** The survey's "own p95" for station-food rising 3.3 → 18.4 ms is real but moderate, while the Server span rises 8×. Most of the growth is therefore in time the service does not attribute to its own code. The volume drop (218 → 40 spans/min) is large and is not explained by the survey, so the tail may partly reflect different traffic mix.

**Bottom line.** The lead's central number (store p95 1.9 → 50.6 ms) is accurate, but the rest of the case does not support "one DB call kind is slow by a steady amount." The list statement on the same connection shows tail growth, the store tail is bursty with a flat median, and a sibling service's DB statements also show tail growth. The better-supported class is a connection-level fault (network_loss/partition, equivalence class), with low confidence. I would not accept `database_call_slow` on this evidence.

Also affected is the food-to-station-food call as seen from the server side, with server p95 rising from 24 to 185 ms, mostly inside station-food's handler. WITH t AS (SELECT 'normal' p, * FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', * FROM abnormal_traces),
pc AS (
 SELECT c.p, par.service_name AS caller, c.service_name AS callee, c.duration, c.attr_status_code, c.attr_http_response_status_code
 FROM t c JOIN t par ON c.parent_span_id = par.span_id AND c.trace_id = par.trace_id AND c.p = par.p
 WHERE c.attr_span_kind IN ('SPAN_KIND_SERVER') AND par.service_name <> c.service_name
)
SELECT p, caller, callee, count(*) n, round(avg(CASE WHEN attr_status_code='STATUS_CODE_ERROR' OR attr_http_response_status_code>=500 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END),3) err,
 round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) p95ms
FROM pc
WHERE callee IN ('ts-food-service','ts-station-food-service','ts-ui-dashboard','ts-preserve-service','ts-travel-service','ts-train-service') OR caller IN ('ts-food-service','ts-station-food-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-ui-dashboard')
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY caller, callee, p

SELECT attr_span_kind, service_name, count(*) n, count(DISTINCT parent_span_id) np FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('ts-food-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-ui-dashboard','ts-station-food-service') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,1

WITH t AS (SELECT 'normal' p, * FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', * FROM abnormal_traces),
pc AS (
 SELECT c.p, par.service_name AS caller, c.service_name AS callee, c.duration, c.attr_status_code, c.attr_http_response_status_code
 FROM t c JOIN t par ON c.parent_span_id = par.span_id AND c.trace_id = par.trace_id AND c.p = par.p
 WHERE c.attr_span_kind = 'Server' AND par.service_name <> c.service_name
)
SELECT p, caller, callee, count(*) n, round(avg(CASE WHEN attr_status_code='Error' OR attr_http_response_status_code>=500 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END),3) err,
 round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) p95ms
FROM pc
WHERE callee IN ('ts-food-service','ts-station-food-service','ts-ui-dashboard','ts-preserve-service','ts-travel-service','ts-train-service') OR caller IN ('ts-food-service','ts-station-food-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-ui-dashboard')
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY caller, callee, p

WITH s AS (SELECT * FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server'),
mn AS (SELECT min(time) t0 FROM abnormal_traces)
SELECT floor(epoch(s.time)-epoch(mn.t0))/60 AS min_bucket,
 sum(CASE WHEN s.service_name='ts-food-service' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) food_in,
 sum(CASE WHEN s.service_name='ts-station-food-service' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) stfood_in,
 sum(CASE WHEN s.service_name='ts-preserve-service' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) preserve_in,
 sum(CASE WHEN s.service_name='ts-ui-dashboard' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ui_in,
 round(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN s.service_name='ts-station-food-service' THEN s.duration END,0.95)/1e6,1) stfood_p95,
 round(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN s.service_name='ts-food-service' THEN s.duration END,0.95)/1e6,1) food_p95
FROM s, mn GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1

**Result: one propagation edge, `ts-preserve-service → ts-ui-dashboard`.** I could not confirm the two food-service edges from the draft as part of this fault's chain.

**Edge kept: `ts-preserve-service → ts-ui-dashboard`**
- Calls from `ts-ui-dashboard` to `ts-preserve-service` went from 0% errors to 100% errors (537 spans in the incident, 84 normal). This is the only link in the data where errors appear.
- The p95 latency is unchanged (1,951 → 1,906 ms). The effect is in the status codes, not in timing, which fits a wrong-status-code fault.

**Links I excluded**
- **`ts-station-food-service → ts-food-service` and `ts-food-service → ts-ui-dashboard` (from the draft):** Both links did change. Food's calls to station-food rose from 23.8 to 185 ms p95 with fewer calls. The ui→food p95 rose from 208 to 295 ms with fewer calls. But neither link is on a route from `ts-preserve-service`. Preserve never calls station-food, and its calls to food stopped rather than degraded. Food's own time also rose (8.7 → 19.7 ms), and station-food's own time rose much more (3.3 → 18.4 ms). The food slowdown therefore looks like a separate problem. I'd treat these two edges as not part of this fault's propagation unless the lead has other evidence.
- **Preserve's callees → preserve (`basic`, `contacts`, `seat`, `security`, `travel`):** Preserve's calls to each rose about 6.4× (21 → 135 per minute), the same ratio as its incoming traffic from the UI. This looks like a volume shift from retries rather than a carried fault. Error rates stayed at 0. Latency changed mixed ways (basic fell, travel rose 547 → 819 ms). I found no error-based link here.
- **Preserve's calls to `assurance`, `food`, `order`, `user`:** These stopped entirely. That comes from the faulty service itself no longer calling them, so nothing travelled to those callees.

**Caveats:** I used about 4 of the ~10 suggested queries. I did not check the per-minute timing of the food degradation against preserve's onset in a clean way, so the exclusion of the food edges rests on the call topology and the onset times in the survey (food at 1 s, station-food at 10 s, preserve at 11 s).

**Answer: two edges.** The fault in `ts-station-food-service` (database_call_slow) reached the users through `ts-food-service` and then `ts-ui-dashboard`. The draft's preserve-service → ui-dashboard edge does not carry this effect.

**Edges (fault-impact direction):**
1. `ts-station-food-service` → `ts-food-service`: `ts-food-service`'s calls to the station-food service fell from 94 to 17 in the trace sample, and p95 rose from 24.6 ms to 191.7 ms. Error share stayed at 0. The callee's own span p95 also rose, from 11 ms to 76 ms. The slowdown is visible on this link.
2. `ts-food-service` → `ts-ui-dashboard`: `ts-ui-dashboard`'s calls to food-service have p95 rising from 213 ms to 347 ms, with volume dropping (205 to 56 sampled calls). Error share stayed at 0. This is the second hop toward the entry service.

**Excluded:**
- `ts-preserve-service` → `ts-ui-dashboard` (in the draft): preserve's calls to the ui-dashboard rose sharply (84 → 537 sampled), but its errors are HTTP 401 and 500 responses. Its p95 to ui-dashboard is flat (2,049 → 1,929 ms). Preserve makes no calls to station-food in the incident period, and its calls to seat, security and travel rose in volume. That points to a separate problem, not the food chain.
- `ts-food-service` → `ts-preserve-service` (in the code's list): preserve's calls to food-service stopped (34 normal, 0 abnormal). Food-service itself was not failing, so a caller going quiet is not evidence that the slowdown travelled to preserve. I left it out, but this is a judgment call and it's the one link I'd want checked if the preserve side matters.

Note: I did not run a separate check on the hubble network metrics. The edges above rest on the trace-level comparisons.
